blocks.en: Unit 8 · Leviticus — Holiness and Worship
blocks.es_reference: Unidad 8 · Levítico — Santidad y Adoración

blocks.en: 1. Why Leviticus Matters
blocks.es_reference: 1. Por Qué Importa Levítico

blocks.en: Leviticus is one of the most avoided books in the Bible for modern Christians, yet it was the first book Hebrew children studied. It is referenced around 40 times in the New Testament. Twenty of its twenty-seven chapters begin with "And the Lord spoke to Moses," evidence conservative scholarship points to as strong support for Mosaic authorship. The Psalms and Proverbs often refer to the offerings described here. If you want to understand the depth of Christ's sacrifice, you must understand Leviticus. The Hebrew word for "sacrifice" is zebah, which means not only sacrifice but also fellowship. Unlike pagan offerings where the god was thought to eat the sacrifice, in Israel's worship, the fat and blood were burned on the altar for God, but most of the meat was returned to the worshiper to share in a communal meal. God hosted His people. The theme of Leviticus is simple: How can a holy God dwell in the midst of a sinful people? The answer is sacrifice — a substitute that covers sin and restores fellowship.
blocks.es_reference: Levítico es uno de los libros más evitados de la Biblia por los cristianos modernos, sin embargo fue el primer libro que estudiaban los niños hebreos. Es referenciado unas 40 veces en el Nuevo Testamento. Veinte de sus veintisiete capítulos comienzan con "Y Jehová habló a Moisés", evidencia que la erudición conservadora señala como fuerte respaldo a la autoría mosaica. Los Salmos y Proverbios a menudo se refieren a las ofrendas descritas aquí. Si quieres entender la profundidad del sacrificio de Cristo, debes entender Levítico. La palabra hebrea para "sacrificio" es zebah, que significa no solo sacrificio sino también comunión. A diferencia de las ofrendas paganas donde se pensaba que el dios comía el sacrificio, en la adoración de Israel, la grasa y la sangre se quemaban en el altar para Dios, pero la mayor parte de la carne se devolvía al adorador para compartir en una comida comunal. Dios hospedaba a Su pueblo. El tema de Levítico es simple: ¿Cómo puede un Dios santo habitar en medio de un pueblo pecador? La respuesta es el sacrificio — un sustituto que cubre el pecado y restaura la comunión.

blocks.en: Leviticus 1:1-2 (NKJV): "Now the Lord called to Moses, and spoke to him from the tabernacle of meeting, saying, 'Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: "When any one of you brings an offering to the Lord, you shall bring your offering of the livestock — of the herd and of the flock."'"
blocks.es_reference: Levítico 1:1-2 (RVG): "Y llamó Jehová a Moisés, y le habló desde el tabernáculo de reunión, diciendo: Habla a los hijos de Israel, y diles: Cuando alguno de vosotros ofreciere ofrenda a Jehová, de ganado vacuno y de ganado menor traeréis vuestra ofrenda."

blocks.en: 2. The Burnt Offering (Leviticus 1): Total Surrender
blocks.es_reference: 2. El Holocausto (Levítico 1): Rendición Total

blocks.en: The burnt offering was made both for atonement and to show appreciation to the Lord. The worshiper brought a male without defect from the herd or flock. He laid his hand on the head of the animal — literally "supporting himself" on it, identifying with the animal as his substitute. This was an intimate act. The worshiper then slaughtered the animal. The priests sprinkled the blood around the altar. The animal was skinned, cut into pieces, and the priest arranged everything on the fire. The entire animal — except the hide given to the priest — was consumed on the altar. The complete consumption symbolized two things: first, it foreshadowed the totality of Christ's sacrifice; second, it signified the worshiper's total dedication to God. The burnt offering is described as "a soothing aroma to the Lord." In pagan cultures, people thought the gods needed to be fed. Not here. God was pleased with the aroma of a devoted heart.
blocks.es_reference: El holocausto se hacía tanto para expiación como para mostrar aprecio al Señor. El adorador traía un macho sin defecto del ganado mayor o menor. Ponía su mano sobre la cabeza del animal — literalmente "apoyándose" en él, identificándose con el animal como su sustituto. Este era un acto íntimo. El adorador entonces degollaba el animal. Los sacerdotes rociaban la sangre alrededor del altar. El animal era desollado, cortado en piezas, y el sacerdote lo disponía todo sobre el fuego. Todo el animal — excepto la piel dada al sacerdote — era consumido en el altar. La consumición total simbolizaba dos cosas: primero, presagiaba la totalidad del sacrificio de Cristo; segundo, significaba la dedicación total del adorador a Dios. El holocausto es descrito como "olor grato a Jehová". En las culturas paganas, la gente pensaba que los dioses necesitaban ser alimentados. No aquí. Dios se complacía en el aroma de un corazón entregado.

blocks.en: 3. The Grain Offering (Leviticus 2): First Fruits and Best Flour
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Ofrenda de Grano (Levítico 2): Primicias y Mejor Harina

blocks.en: The grain offering was often supplemental to burnt offerings, or could be a sin offering for the very poor. It consisted of fine flour, oil, and frankincense. A handful was burned on the altar as a memorial portion, and the remainder went to the priests for food. Nothing with leaven or honey could be offered. Leaven symbolized corruption. Every grain offering was seasoned with salt — "the salt of the covenant of your God." Salt preserves and purifies. The first fruits offering brought fresh heads of grain roasted in the fire. The beauty here is that even the poorest Israelite could bring an offering. No one was excluded from worship due to poverty.
blocks.es_reference: La ofrenda de grano a menudo era suplementaria a los holocaustos, o podía ser una ofrenda de pecado para los muy pobres. Consistía en harina fina, aceite e incienso. Un puñado se quemaba en el altar como porción memorial, y el resto iba a los sacerdotes para alimento. No se podía ofrecer nada con levadura ni miel. La levadura simbolizaba la corrupción. Toda ofrenda de grano se sazonaba con sal — "la sal del pacto de tu Dios". La sal conserva y purifica. La ofrenda de primicias traía espigas frescas tostadas al fuego. La belleza aquí es que incluso el israelita más pobre podía traer una ofrenda. Nadie quedaba excluido de la adoración por pobreza.

blocks.en: Pastoral Note: The grain offering teaches that worship costs something — you bring your best, not your leftovers. But it also teaches that God provides for those who serve Him (the priests ate the remainder). Give God your first and best, and trust Him to take care of the rest.
blocks.es_reference: Nota Pastoral: La ofrenda de grano enseña que la adoración cuesta algo — traes lo mejor, no las sobras. Pero también enseña que Dios provee para los que le sirven (los sacerdotes comían el resto). Dale a Dios lo primero y lo mejor, y confía que Él cuidará del resto.

blocks.en: 4. The Peace or Fellowship Offering (Leviticus 3): Celebration and Communion
blocks.es_reference: 4. La Ofrenda de Paz o Comunión (Levítico 3): Celebración y Comunión

blocks.en: The Hebrew word for "peace" (shalom) means wholeness, completeness, soundness, health. When you have these things in full, you are at peace. The peace offering was a time of great fellowship — eating, drinking, talking, and singing. Not what one usually thinks of when one thinks of "sacrifice." The worshiper brought an animal without defect, male or female. He laid his hand on its head and slaughtered it. The fat, the kidneys (viewed as the center of emotion), and the lobe of the liver (which pagans thought controlled the future) were burned on the altar. By offering these, the worshiper was effectively giving to God all his emotions and trusting Him with the future. The rest of the meat was consumed by the worshiper and his family in a festive meal. The order was often: first a burnt offering (atonement), then a peace offering (fellowship). Once sin was dealt with, celebration could begin. God gave the majority of the meat back to the worshiper — grace on full display.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra hebrea para "paz" (shalom) significa plenitud, completitud, salud, bienestar. Cuando tienes estas cosas en plenitud, estás en paz. La ofrenda de paz era un tiempo de gran comunión — comer, beber, conversar y cantar. No lo que uno piensa normalmente cuando piensa en "sacrificio". El adorador traía un animal sin defecto, macho o hembra. Ponía su mano sobre su cabeza y lo degollaba. La grasa, los riñones (vistos como el centro de la emoción) y el lóbulo del hígado (que los paganos pensaban que controlaba el futuro) se quemaban en el altar. Al ofrecer estos, el adorador estaba efectivamente dando a Dios todas sus emociones y confiándole el futuro. El resto de la carne era consumido por el adorador y su familia en una comida festiva. El orden era a menudo: primero un holocausto (expiación), luego una ofrenda de paz (comunión). Una vez que el pecado estaba tratado, podía comenzar la celebración. Dios devolvía la mayor parte de la carne al adorador — gracia en plena exhibición.

blocks.en: 5. The Sin Offering (Leviticus 4): Unintentional Sins Covered
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Ofrenda por el Pecado (Levítico 4): Pecados No Intencionales Cubiertos

blocks.en: The sin offering dealt with unintentional sins — things done without knowing they were wrong. The Hebrew word translated "if" in "If a person sins unintentionally" is better translated "when." It's assumed we will make unintentional mistakes. The offering varied based on who sinned. For the anointed priest or the whole congregation: a bull without defect. For a leader: a male goat. For a common person: a female goat or lamb. The more public the sin's impact, the greater the offering. The priest dipped his finger in the blood and sprinkled it seven times before the veil (for priest or nation — in the Holy Place). For a leader or common person, the blood was put on the horns of the altar of burnt offering (in the courtyard). The fat was burned, but the rest of the animal was burned outside the camp for the priest or nation's offering — so that no one would profit from a sin offering. For the common person, the meat could be eaten by the priests. Notice the progression: the more responsible the person, the stricter the requirement. But in every case, forgiveness was available. Paul would later say, "Where sin abounded, grace abounded much more" (Romans 5:20).
blocks.es_reference: La ofrenda por el pecado trataba con pecados no intencionales — cosas hechas sin saber que estaban mal. La palabra hebrea traducida "si" en "Si una persona pecare por yerro" se traduce mejor como "cuando". Se asume que cometeremos errores no intencionales. La ofrenda variaba según quién pecaba. Para el sacerdote ungido o toda la congregación: un becerro sin defecto. Para un líder: un macho cabrío. Para una persona común: una hembra de cabra o cordero. Cuanto más público era el impacto del pecado, mayor era la ofrenda. El sacerdote mojaba su dedo en la sangre y la rociaba siete veces delante del velo (para el sacerdote o la nación — en el Lugar Santo). Para un líder o persona común, la sangre se ponía en los cuernos del altar del holocausto (en el atrio). La grasa se quemaba, pero el resto del animal se quemaba fuera del campamento para la ofrenda del sacerdote o la nación — para que nadie se beneficiara de una ofrenda por el pecado. Para la persona común, la carne podía ser comida por los sacerdotes. Observa la progresión: cuanto más responsable es la persona, más estricto es el requisito. Pero en cada caso, el perdón estaba disponible. Pablo diría más tarde: "Donde el pecado abundó, sobreabundó la gracia" (Romanos 5:20).

blocks.en: Leviticus 4:27-28 (NKJV): "If any one of the common people sins unintentionally by doing something against any of the commandments of the Lord... he shall bring as his offering a female goat without blemish for his sin which he has committed."
blocks.es_reference: Levítico 4:27-28 (RVG): "Y si alguna persona del común del pueblo pecare por yerro, haciendo algo contra alguno de los mandamientos de Jehová... traerá por su ofrenda una cabra sin defecto, hembra, por su pecado que cometió."

blocks.en: 6. The Guilt Offering (Leviticus 5-6): Restitution and Forgiveness
blocks.es_reference: 6. La Ofrenda por la Culpa (Levítico 5-6): Restitución y Perdón

blocks.en: The guilt offering applied to sins against the Lord's holy things or sins against a neighbor. If someone sinned by failing to testify when they had knowledge, or by touching something unclean, or by swearing thoughtlessly, they had to confess and bring a female lamb or goat. If too poor, two turtledoves. If even too poor for that, fine flour — no oil or incense. Notice: God made provision for the poorest person. No one was beyond the reach of forgiveness. But the guilt offering also required restitution. If someone defrauded a neighbor, he had to restore what was taken plus add a fifth (20%) and then bring the guilt offering. When we sin against another person, we have acted unfaithfully against the Lord. Forgiveness does not remove the responsibility to make things right. This is why Jesus said, "If you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there... first be reconciled to your brother" (Matthew 5:23-24).
blocks.es_reference: La ofrenda por la culpa se aplicaba a pecados contra las cosas santas de Jehová o pecados contra el prójimo. Si alguien pecaba por no testificar cuando tenía conocimiento, o por tocar algo inmundo, o por jurar imprudentemente, tenía que confesar y traer una cordera o cabra hembra. Si era demasiado pobre, dos tórtolas. Si incluso demasiado pobre para eso, harina fina — sin aceite ni incienso. Observa: Dios hizo provisión para la persona más pobre. Nadie estaba fuera del alcance del perdón. Pero la ofrenda por la culpa también requería restitución. Si alguien defraudaba a su prójimo, tenía que restaurar lo tomado más añadir una quinta parte (20%) y luego traer la ofrenda por la culpa. Cuando pecamos contra otra persona, hemos actuado infielmente contra el Señor. El perdón no elimina la responsabilidad de restaurar lo que está roto. Por eso Jesús dijo: "Si traes tu ofrenda al altar y allí te acuerdas de que tu hermano tiene algo contra ti, deja allí tu ofrenda... reconcíliate primero con tu hermano" (Mateo 5:23-24).

blocks.en: 7. The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16): The Most Holy Day
blocks.es_reference: 7. El Día de la Expiación (Levítico 16): El Día Más Santo

blocks.en: Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest entered the Holy of Holies — the only time anyone could enter. He first offered a bull as a sin offering for himself and his household. Then he took two goats. One goat was sacrificed as a sin offering for the people. Its blood was brought into the Holy of Holies and sprinkled on the mercy seat (the cover of the Ark of the Covenant). The high priest laid his hands on the head of the second goat — the scapegoat — confessed over it all the sins of Israel, and sent it away into the wilderness, bearing their sins to a desolate land. This was a powerful picture: the blood of the sacrificed goat paid the penalty for sin; the scapegoat visibly removed the sin from the camp. Both pointed to Jesus. Hebrews 9 explains: Christ entered the heavenly Holy of Holies once for all with His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption. And He bore our sins outside the camp. The Day of Atonement was the climax of Israel's worship year — the day when the high priest, the people, and even the tabernacle itself were cleansed.
blocks.es_reference: Una vez al año, el décimo día del séptimo mes, el sumo sacerdote entraba en el Lugar Santísimo — la única vez que alguien podía entrar. Primero ofrecía un becerro como ofrenda por el pecado para sí mismo y su casa. Luego tomaba dos machos cabríos. Un macho cabrío era sacrificado como ofrenda por el pecado del pueblo. Su sangre era llevada al Lugar Santísimo y rociada sobre el propiciatorio (la cubierta del Arca del Pacto). El sumo sacerdote ponía sus manos sobre la cabeza del segundo macho cabrío — el chivo expiatorio — confesaba sobre él todos los pecados de Israel, y lo enviaba al desierto, llevando sus pecados a una tierra desolada. Esta era una imagen poderosa: la sangre del macho cabrío sacrificado pagaba la pena del pecado; el chivo expiatorio eliminaba visiblemente el pecado del campamento. Ambos apuntaban a Jesús. Hebreos 9 explica: Cristo entró en el Lugar Santísimo celestial una vez para siempre con Su propia sangre, obteniendo eterna redención. Y llevó nuestros pecados fuera del campamento. El Día de la Expiación era el punto culminante del año de adoración de Israel — el día en que el sumo sacerdote, el pueblo, e incluso el tabernáculo mismo eran purificados.

blocks.en: Christ Connection: Jesus is both our sacrifice and our scapegoat. He died in our place (the sacrificed goat) and He carried our sins away (the scapegoat). As the writer of Hebrews says, "He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption" (Hebrews 9:12).
blocks.es_reference: Conexión con Cristo: Jesús es tanto nuestro sacrificio como nuestro chivo expiatorio. Murió en nuestro lugar (el macho cabrío sacrificado) y llevó nuestros pecados lejos (el chivo expiatorio). Como dice el escritor de Hebreos: "Él entró una sola vez en el Lugar Santísimo por su propia sangre, habiendo obtenido eterna redención" (Hebreos 9:12).

blocks.en: Leviticus 16:21-22 (NKJV): "Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel... and he shall release the goat in the wilderness. The goat shall bear on itself all their iniquities to an uninhabited land."
blocks.es_reference: Levítico 16:21-22 (RVG): "Y pondrá Aarón sus dos manos sobre la cabeza del macho cabrío vivo, y confesará sobre él todas las iniquidades de los hijos de Israel... y lo soltará por el desierto. Y aquel macho cabrío llevará sobre sí todas las iniquidades de ellos a tierra inhabitada."

blocks.en: 8. The Priests' Portion: Living from the Offerings
blocks.es_reference: 8. La Porción de los Sacerdotes: Viviendo de las Ofrendas

blocks.en: Leviticus 6-7 gives detailed instructions for the priests. The burnt offering remained on the hearth all night. The priest's linen garments were holy and could not be worn outside the tabernacle. The fire on the altar was to be kept burning continually — it was never to go out. This symbolizes that access to God through sacrifice is never closed. The priests could eat the grain offering (except when offering for themselves), the sin offering (except when blood was brought into the Holy Place), and the guilt offering. The breast and right thigh of the peace offering belonged to the priests. God provided for His servants through the worship of His people. This is the biblical pattern for ministry support.
blocks.es_reference: Levítico 6-7 da instrucciones detalladas para los sacerdotes. El holocausto permanecía en el hogar toda la noche. Las vestiduras de lino del sacerdote eran santas y no podían usarse fuera del tabernáculo. El fuego del altar debía mantenerse encendido continuamente — nunca debía apagarse. Esto simboliza que el acceso a Dios a través del sacrificio nunca se cierra. Los sacerdotes podían comer la ofrenda de grano (excepto cuando ofrecían por sí mismos), la ofrenda por el pecado (excepto cuando la sangre era llevada al Lugar Santo) y la ofrenda por la culpa. El pecho y la espaldilla derecha de la ofrenda de paz pertenecían a los sacerdotes. Dios proveía para Sus siervos a través de la adoración de Su pueblo. Este es el patrón bíblico para el sustento del ministerio.

blocks.en: 9. What the Sacrifices Teach Us About Forgiveness
blocks.es_reference: 9. Lo Que los Sacrificios Nos Enseñan Sobre el Perdón

blocks.en: The sacrificial system was never intended to save — "it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins" (Hebrews 10:4). So what was its purpose? First, it taught that sin is deadly and requires a substitute. Second, it pictured the coming sacrifice of Christ. Third, it provided a way for the worshiper to experience forgiveness and restored fellowship by faith. When an Israelite laid his hand on the animal's head, he was saying, "This animal dies in my place." When he ate the peace offering meal, he was celebrating that God had accepted him. And when the scapegoat vanished into the wilderness, he knew his sin was gone. The sacrifice did not earn forgiveness — it received it by faith, looking forward to the cross. Your congregation needs to understand that Leviticus is not a tedious rulebook but a beautiful gospel drama acted out in blood, fire, and fellowship meals.
blocks.es_reference: El sistema sacrificial nunca tuvo la intención de salvar — "la sangre de los toros y de los machos cabríos no puede quitar los pecados" (Hebreos 10:4). Entonces, ¿cuál era su propósito? Primero, enseñaba que el pecado es mortal y requiere un sustituto. Segundo, representaba el sacrificio venidero de Cristo. Tercero, proporcionaba una manera para que el adorador experimentara el perdón y la comunión restaurada por fe. Cuando un israelita ponía su mano sobre la cabeza del animal, estaba diciendo: "Este animal muere en mi lugar". Cuando comía la comida de la ofrenda de paz, celebraba que Dios lo había aceptado. Y cuando el chivo expiatorio desaparecía en el desierto, sabía que su pecado había desaparecido. El sacrificio no ganaba el perdón — lo recibía por fe, esperando la cruz. Tu congregación necesita entender que Levítico no es un libro de reglas tedioso sino un hermoso drama del evangelio actuado con sangre, fuego y comidas de comunión.

blocks.en: 10. Grace in Every Sacrifice: For Rich and Poor Alike
blocks.es_reference: 10. Gracia en Cada Sacrificio: Para Ricos y Pobres por Igual

blocks.en: Notice throughout Leviticus that God made provision for every economic level. The wealthy brought a bull. The middle class brought a lamb or goat. The poor brought two turtledoves. The very poor brought fine flour. No one was turned away because they could not afford an expensive sacrifice. The poor man's flour was just as acceptable as the rich man's bull because both were offered in faith. This is grace. The world measures access by wealth; God measures access by faith. The same blood (or flour representing a bloodless sacrifice for the poorest) covered all. And when you understand that all of this pointed to Jesus, you realize that in Christ, the richest and the poorest come to the cross on the same ground: grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.
blocks.es_reference: Observa a lo largo de Levítico que Dios hizo provisión para cada nivel económico. El rico traía un becerro. La clase media traía un cordero o cabra. El pobre traía dos tórtolas. El muy pobre traía harina fina. Nadie era rechazado porque no podía pagar un sacrificio costoso. La harina del pobre era tan aceptable como el becerro del rico porque ambos se ofrecían con fe. Esto es gracia. El mundo mide el acceso por la riqueza; Dios mide el acceso por la fe. La misma sangre (o harina que representa un sacrificio incruento para los más pobres) cubría a todos. Y cuando entiendes que todo esto apuntaba a Jesús, te das cuenta de que en Cristo, el más rico y el más pobre llegan a la cruz en el mismo terreno: gracia solamente, por fe solamente, en Cristo solamente.

blocks.en: Application for Pastors: Preach Leviticus! Show your people that the Old Testament is not obsolete — it is the foundation that makes the New Testament glorious. Every time you administer communion, you are saying, "Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us." The bread and wine echo the peace offering meal. Help your congregation see the gospel in every page.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación para Pastores: ¡Predica Levítico! Muestra a tu pueblo que el Antiguo Testamento no está obsoleto — es el fundamento que hace glorioso el Nuevo Testamento. Cada vez que administras la comunión, estás diciendo: "Cristo, nuestra pascua, fue sacrificado por nosotros". El pan y el vino hacen eco de la comida de la ofrenda de paz. Ayuda a tu congregación a ver el evangelio en cada página.

mc.stem: What book of the Bible was the first book Hebrew children studied?
mc.why: Correct! Leviticus was the first book Hebrew children studied, yet modern Christians avoid it.

mc.stem: The Hebrew word for sacrifice, 'zebah,' also carries what meaning?
mc.why: Yes. Zebah means sacrifice but also fellowship — God hosted His people with a meal.

mc.stem: In the burnt offering, the worshiper laid his hand on the animal's head to signify what?
mc.why: Correct. He was 'supporting himself' on the animal, identifying with it as his substitute.

mc.stem: The complete consumption of the burnt offering symbolized what two things?
options: Christ's total sacrifice and the worshiper's total dedication
mc.why: Yes. The burnt offering pointed to Christ's complete sacrifice and called for total surrender.

mc.stem: What could not be offered in a grain offering because it symbolized corruption?
mc.why: Correct. Leaven symbolized corruption and was forbidden in grain offerings.

mc.stem: Every grain offering was seasoned with what, called 'the salt of the covenant'?
mc.why: Yes. Salt preserves and purifies — a reminder of the covenant's permanence.

mc.stem: The peace or fellowship offering was a time of what?
mc.why: Yes. The peace offering was festive — a meal celebrating restored fellowship with God.

mc.stem: What was offered on the altar from the peace offering, and what did this symbolize?
options: The fat, kidneys, and liver — emotions and future to God
mc.why: Correct. The fat (best portion), kidneys (emotions), and liver (future) were given to God.

mc.stem: The sin offering in Leviticus 4 primarily dealt with what kind of sins?
mc.why: Yes. The sin offering covered unintentional sins — things done without knowing they were wrong.

mc.stem: For a common person, what animal was offered as a sin offering?
mc.why: Correct. A female goat or lamb — God made provision for everyone.

mc.stem: Why was the animal burned outside the camp for the priest's or nation's sin offering?
options: So no one would profit from a sin offering
mc.why: Yes. Burning outside the camp ensured no one economically benefited from a sin offering.

mc.stem: What did the guilt offering require in addition to the animal sacrifice?
mc.why: Correct. Restitution (restoring what was taken plus a fifth) was required before forgiveness.

mc.stem: Jesus referenced the principle of the guilt offering when He said what in Matthew 5?
options: 'First be reconciled to your brother, then come offer your gift'
mc.why: Yes. Jesus taught that worship requires reconciled relationships — the same principle as the guilt offering.

mc.stem: How often was the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) observed?
mc.why: Correct. Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month — the holiest day of Israel's calendar.

mc.stem: What was done with the scapegoat on the Day of Atonement?
options: It was sacrificed on the altar
It was sent into the wilderness bearing the sins of the people

mc.stem: The blood of the sacrificed goat on the Day of Atonement was sprinkled on what?

mc.stem: What does Hebrews 9 say about Christ's sacrifice in relation to the Day of Atonement?

Christ entered heaven's Holy of Holies once for all with His own blood
mc.why: Yes! Christ's once-for-all sacrifice fulfilled what the Day of Atonement pictured.

mc.stem: What was to be kept burning continually on the altar?
mc.why: Correct. The fire was never to go out — access to God through sacrifice is always open.

mc.stem: God made provision for the very poorest person to bring what as a sin offering?

mc.stem: According to Hebrews 10:4, what could the blood of bulls and goats NOT do?

sa.prompt: Why is Leviticus important for Christians today, despite being often avoided?
sa.model: Leviticus is referenced 40 times in the NT and is essential for understanding Christ's sacrifice as our High Priest and substitute.

sa.prompt: Describe the burnt offering — what it symbolized and how it was performed.
sa.model: A male without defect, hand laid on head identifying substitute, entire animal burned — symbolizing total dedication and pointing to Christ's total sacrifice.

sa.prompt: What made the grain offering accessible to the poor, and what did the salt represent?
sa.model: The poorest could bring fine flour. Salt represented the preserving, purifying nature of God's covenant.

sa.prompt: What was the peace offering, and how did it demonstrate God's grace?
sa.model: A celebratory meal where most of the meat was returned to the worshiper — God hosted His people in grace.

sa.prompt: How did the sin offering vary based on who sinned, and why?
sa.model: The more public the sin's impact, the greater the offering — greater responsibility requires stricter atonement.

sa.prompt: What two things did the guilt offering require beyond the sacrifice itself?
sa.model: Restitution (return what was taken) plus adding 20% — showing that forgiveness doesn't remove responsibility to make things right.

sa.prompt: Describe the two goats on the Day of Atonement and what each represented.
sa.model: One sacrificed — blood on mercy seat (penalty paid). One scapegoat — sins sent away (guilt removed). Both point to Christ.

sa.prompt: What did the perpetual fire on the altar symbolize?
sa.model: Access to God through sacrifice was never closed — a picture of God's constant readiness to receive repentant sinners.

sa.prompt: How did God make forgiveness accessible to every economic level in Israel?
sa.model: God provided a sliding scale of offerings — from a bull to fine flour — so no one was turned away due to poverty.

sa.prompt: According to Hebrews 9-10, how does Christ's sacrifice surpass the Old Testament sacrificial system?
sa.model: Christ's sacrifice is once-for-all, never to be repeated, using His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption, and giving us direct access to God.
